# F4 (part B): The one-shot holdout

*Generated by `python -m forecast.render_f4_holdout` from `results/f4_holdout.json` and
`results/f4_backtest.json`. Do not edit the numbers by hand.*

## What this step does, in plain words

Part A chose and froze the model using only the backtest windows. This step tests that frozen model
once on the last 28 days of the data, d_1914..d_1941 (2016-04-25 to 2016-05-22).
Nothing before had read, scored or tuned on those days. The model and every F3 baseline forecast from
the same day (d_1913) with the same metrics, so the result shows how they do on genuinely new data.

**Headline:** On the 28 unseen days the global LightGBM model has a WRMSSE of **0.798**, against **0.839** for TSB (the best baseline in the backtest) and 1.055 for seasonal naive: 4.8% lower than TSB (backtest: 4.9% lower).

On the holdout the best baseline is SBA (0.833), not TSB (0.839). The comparison baseline was fixed before the run (the best in the backtest), so TSB stays the reference; against SBA the model is 4.2% lower. The baselines are close together (0.833 to 0.846 for the smoothing rules), as in F3.

## How it was run

- **From a frozen commit.** `python -m forecast.run_f4_holdout` ran once, from commit `1a31ed9`
  (`1a31ed9d230b638284fcbbfb118dd80740c6ca0b`), started 2026-10-15T12:18:52+00:00. It refuses to run if the git tree is not clean, and refuses
  a second run because `results/f4_holdout.json` now exists.
- **The frozen model.** Setting s1_small: 31 leaves, learning rate 0.05, at least 100
  rows per leaf, 200 trees. These come from `config/model_final.yaml`, chosen on the backtest
  only. It was trained on 4,087,167 rows, all with target days up to d_1913, and forecasts
  d_1914..d_1941 from d_1913. The run took 1.1 min.
- **What was scored.** 5,748 of 5,748 series (160,944 listed series-days); at the
  origin: smooth 531, erratic 274, intermittent 3,360, lumpy 1,583. Unlisted days are not scored, as in F3.

| TSB | 0.839 | 0.873 | -0.034 | 0.791 | 1.429 | -0.050 | -2.4% | 34.9% |

![Holdout vs backtest](figures/f4_holdout_vs_backtest.png)

The model ranks first of 8 methods on the holdout. It is 24.3% lower than seasonal naive. Every method scores better on the holdout than its backtest average, so the level of the numbers moves with the period. The comparison is about the order and the gaps between methods on the same days.

## 5. Bias and weekly totals for the whole slice

| Week | Actual units | LightGBM (global) (error) | TSB (error) | Seasonal naive (error) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 81,008 | 78,336 (-3.3%) | 82,874 (+2.3%) | 80,289 (-0.9%) |
| 2 | 85,838 | 83,021 (-3.3%) | 82,874 (-3.5%) | 80,289 (-6.5%) |
| 3 | 87,169 | 81,985 (-5.9%) | 82,874 (-4.9%) | 80,289 (-7.9%) |
| 4 | 85,546 | 79,558 (-7.0%) | 82,874 (-3.1%) | 80,289 (-6.1%) |

Over the whole holdout the model's slice total is -4.9% against the actual
(TSB: -2.4%). Its weekly errors range from -7.0% to -3.3%
(TSB: -4.9% to +2.3%), and it is below the actual in 4 of 4 weeks. The model under-forecasts the slice total, as in the backtest (-4.3%). Per series it is more accurate, but F5 should size safety stock from the residuals, not assume an unbiased forecast.

## 6. Limits of this test

- **One window.** The holdout is a single 28-day period from one origin (2016-04-25 to 2016-05-22). The
  backtest's 4 origins show how much results move between windows; one holdout window cannot.
- **Item-store level only.** WRMSSE here averages item-store series only (as in F3). It is not the
  M5 leaderboard score, which also averages 11 aggregate levels.
- **Simulated use, not deployment.** The model forecasts once from a fixed day. A store would
  re-forecast as new days arrive.

## 7. Handed to F5

Forecasts, actuals and residuals (actual − forecast) per series, horizon and method on the holdout
(1,287,552 rows) are in `data/processed/f4_holdout_forecasts.parquet` (gitignored; per-item data is not redistributed). The backtest
residuals from part A are next to them, for sizing safety stock without using the holdout.
